title: Brokerage (ALyC) Commission Calculator + Table | Hacé Cuentas
description: Calculate the real cost of trading in a brokerage account: broker commission, exchange (market) fees and VAT. Enter the traded amount and commission rate to get your total cost and net amount instantly.
answerSnippet: Total trading cost = broker commission + exchange fees + VAT. Commission = amount × commission%/100; exchange (market) fees ≈ amount × 0.08%; VAT = (commission + fees) × 21%. Example: trading $1,000,000 at a 0.5% commission costs $5,000 + $800 fees + $1,218 VAT = $7,018 total (0.70% of the amount).
seoKeywords: how much does a broker charge
intro: Every time you buy or sell stocks, bonds, ETFs or any security in your brokerage account, your broker (an **ALyC** — Agent for Settlement and Clearing — in Argentina) charges a **commission**, plus **exchange (market) fees** and **VAT** on top. These costs look small as a percentage but are deducted on every trade and erode your real return. This calculator shows exactly what you pay: enter the amount you're trading and your broker's commission rate, and get the full breakdown — commission, exchange fees, VAT — plus the total cost and the net amount (what you disburse when buying or receive when selling). Defaults reflect the Argentine market (0.5% commission, 0.08% BYMA fees, 21% VAT); edit them to match your broker and jurisdiction.
keyTakeaway: **See the real cost of every trade.** Brokerage commissions look tiny (0.5% is typical), but once you add exchange fees and VAT the total runs around 0.70% per side — and a round trip (buy + sell) nearly doubles it. Use this to know exactly what your broker takes.

example.title: Example: trading $1,000,000 in stocks at a 0.5% commission
steps: Traded amount: $1,000,000 · Commission: 0.5% · Exchange fees: 0.08% · VAT: 21%
Buying you'd disburse $1,007,018; selling you'd net $992,982

explanation:
## How the trading cost is calculated

The total cost of a trade in a brokerage account has three components:

```
commission   = traded_amount × commission% / 100
exch_fees    = traded_amount × fees% / 100        (exchange/clearing, ~0.08% for stocks)
VAT          = (commission + exch_fees) × VAT% / 100
total_cost   = commission + exch_fees + VAT
```

The **net amount** depends on the side of the trade:

```
buying:   you disburse = amount + total_cost
selling:  you receive  = amount − total_cost
```

> **Round trip cost matters most.** A position that you open and later close pays costs twice — once buying, once selling. At 0.5% commission, a $100,000 round trip costs roughly $1,400, which is the minimum return your trade must generate just to break even.

---

## Cost reference table

Total cost per **$100,000 traded** (0.08% exchange fees + 21% VAT), by commission rate:

| Commission | Total cost | % of amount |
|------------|------------|-------------|
| 0.3% | $460 | 0.46% |
| 0.5% | $702 | 0.70% |
| 0.6% | $823 | 0.82% |
| 1.0% | $1,307 | 1.31% |

*Scale linearly for other amounts. A round trip (buy + sell) costs roughly twice this.*

---

## What each charge is

- **Broker commission:** what the broker charges to execute the order. Each broker has its own schedule; stock commissions in Argentina usually run **0.3%–0.6%**, sometimes with a fixed minimum per trade (e.g., $50–$200 ARS minimum regardless of amount). Large institutional clients often negotiate lower rates; retail clients generally pay the published schedule. Commissions are set by each broker and are **not regulated at a fixed rate** by CNV — compare brokers before opening an account.

- **Exchange (market) fees:** charged by the exchange and clearing house for using market infrastructure and settlement. In Argentina the main venues are **BYMA** (Bolsas y Mercados Argentinos, for stocks, CEDEARs and ETFs) and **MAE** (Mercado Abierto Electrónico, for most bonds and short-term government securities). These fees vary by instrument type and are set by the exchanges, not the broker. The **~0.08% figure applies to equities**; bond transactions at MAE carry different rate structures, so verify with your broker when trading fixed income.

- **VAT (IVA):** brokerage intermediation is a taxable financial service in Argentina, subject to **21% IVA** applied on commission plus exchange fees — not on the traded amount itself. Set this field to 0 if your jurisdiction does not tax brokerage services, or if you are a VAT-registered entity that can recover it.

---

## What this calculator does NOT include

These real costs exist and affect your actual return, but are outside the scope of this tool:

- **Stamp duty / Impuesto de sellos:** some Argentine provinces apply a stamp tax on financial transactions. Buenos Aires province is the most common example; check your broker's settlement summary to see if it applies to your account.
- **Capital gains tax (Impuesto a las Ganancias / Cedular):** profits on Argentine equities held by individuals are generally exempt for Argentine residents (as of current legislation), but CEDEARs and foreign assets may have different treatment. Consult a tax advisor.
- **Bid-ask spread:** the difference between the price at which you can buy and the price at which you can sell at any given moment. On liquid large-cap stocks this may be 0.05%–0.1%; on illiquid small caps or bonds it can be 1%–5% or more. This is a real cost that never appears on your commission invoice.
- **FX conversion costs:** if you trade CEDEARs or dollar-denominated assets and need to convert ARS↔USD, the implicit exchange rate used by your broker may differ from the reference rate.
- **Custody or maintenance fees:** some brokers charge a monthly or annual account fee, especially for inactivity. Not all do.

---

## Common mistakes

**1. Applying the commission rate to the net amount instead of the gross.**
Commission is always calculated on the full traded amount (before subtracting costs), not on what you ultimately receive. This calculator uses the correct convention.

**2. Forgetting the round trip.**
Evaluating a trade only on entry cost understates total drag by half. Always model both legs before deciding whether a trade makes economic sense.

**3. Assuming all instruments carry the same exchange fee.**
The ~0.08% default is appropriate for BYMA-listed equities. Bonds, short-term bills (Letras), and other instruments may carry materially different exchange and settlement fees. When in doubt, ask your broker for the full fee schedule per instrument type.

**4. Ignoring the minimum commission.**
If your broker charges a minimum of, say, $150 ARS per trade, and you trade $10,000 ARS worth of stock, your effective commission rate is far higher than the quoted percentage. The minimum per-trade floor matters most on small orders.

---

## Practical context

For a **long-term buy-and-hold investor** making a handful of trades per year, total commission costs are modest relative to market returns. For an **active trader** turning over their portfolio frequently, accumulated commissions become a significant drag — at 0.5% per side, 20 round trips per year on a $500,000 portfolio costs roughly $100,000 in commissions alone, before spreads.

Comparing brokers on commission rate is useful, but also check execution quality, platform reliability, and the scope of instruments available — a cheaper broker that can't access the instruments you need provides no real saving.

faq.a: It's the investment account you open with a broker to buy and sell financial assets — stocks, bonds, ETFs, money-market funds, currencies. In Argentina it's called a 'cuenta comitente' held at an ALyC, with custody at Caja de Valores. Every trade you make in it generates commissions and fees.

faq.q: How much does a broker charge in commission to trade stocks?
faq.a: It depends on the broker. Stock commissions commonly run 0.3%–0.6% of the traded amount, and many brokers apply a fixed minimum per trade. Some brokers offer 0% commission on certain instruments (their own funds, for example) but make it up elsewhere. Always check the current fee schedule.

They are charges by the exchange and clearing house — BYMA for stocks and ETFs, MAE for many bonds in Argentina — for negotiation, registration, settlement, and custody of the trade. They vary by security; around 0.08% of the amount for stocks. They appear itemized on your trade confirmation.

faq.q: Is there a tax on trading?
faq.a: In Argentina, brokerage intermediation is subject to 21% VAT, applied on the commission plus the exchange fees (not on the full traded amount). Other countries tax brokerage differently or not at all — set the VAT field to your local rate, or 0 if it doesn't apply.

faq.q: What's the real cost of trading $1,000,000?
faq.a: At 0.5% commission, 0.08% exchange fees and 21% VAT: commission is $5,000, fees $800, and VAT on ($5,000 + $800) is $1,218. Total cost is $7,018 — 0.70% of the amount. Buying you'd disburse $1,007,018; selling you'd net $992,982.

faq.q: How far must an asset rise before I profit after fees?
faq.a: You pay the cost on both the buy and the sell. At 0.70% per side, a round trip costs about 1.4%. The asset must rise at least 1.4% just to cover commissions and taxes before you start making money. This is why trading very often eats into returns.

faq.q: Why do minimum commissions hurt small trades?
faq.a: Many brokers charge a fixed minimum per trade. On a small amount, that minimum can represent a far higher percentage than the headline rate. A $10 minimum on a $500 trade equals 2% — well above a 0.5% rate. For small amounts, look for a broker with no minimum or a low floor.

faq.q: Are commissions the same for stocks, bonds and currencies?
faq.a: No. Each instrument has its own commission and exchange-fee schedule. Bonds usually carry lower commissions than stocks, repos have their own structure, and currency trades (like dólar MEP) may be commission-free or have a specific fee. Adjust the percentages in the calculator to match the instrument and your broker.

dataUpdate.notes: Commission and exchange-fee rates are editable in the calculator. Default values (0.5% commission, 0.08% BYMA fees, 21% VAT) are reviewed when BYMA tariffs or tax rules change.
